segs.text: Module eight, objective one. Linear versus nonlinear pharmacokinetics. In linear pharmacokinetics the parameters, such as the half life and the clearance, do not change when different or multiple doses of a drug are given. In nonlinear pharmacokinetics, increased doses or chronic administration cause deviations from the profile seen with single doses, and the half life and the clearance change. She said, Linear, our parameters don't change, nonlinear, they do. Phenytoin is the prototype nonlinear drug in this course.

card.m: linear: t<sub>½</sub>, Cl unchanged with dose
nonlinear: higher or repeated doses → t<sub>½</sub>, Cl change
Ex. phenytoin

segs.text: Most drugs are eliminated by a first order process, which is linear. The amount removed per unit of time is proportional to the amount present, so the fraction removed per unit of time stays the same at every level. Because that fraction is fixed, the half life and the clearance are the same at every dose. So twice the dose gives twice the level at every time and twice the A U C, the area under the curve of level against time, and repeated doses can be predicted from the first dose by superposition: each new dose adds its own curve to what is left of the earlier ones.

card.m: first order: amount removed per time ∝ amount present; fraction per time constant
→ t<sub>½</sub>, Cl the same at every dose
2 × dose → 2 × level, 2 × AUC (AUC ∝ dose); superposition

segs.text: Nonlinear pharmacokinetics comes from saturation of an enzyme or carrier system that can only work so fast. V max, the fastest elimination rate it can reach, is a rate: an amount or concentration per unit of time. K M is the concentration at which the rate is half of V max, and the drug level, C p, is low or high only compared with K M. Well below K M, the rate is a small part of V max, so the enzymes have spare capacity, and twice the level gives about twice the rate: first order. Well above K M, the enzymes are saturated: more drug raises the rate only a little, so it stays near V max: zero order. She said, That's as fast as it can go.

card.m: cause: a saturable enzyme or carrier
V<sub>max</sub>: the fastest elimination rate, a rate (her example 12 mg/kg/day)
K<sub>M</sub>: the concentration at which rate = ½ V<sub>max</sub> (her example 10 mg/L)
C<sub>p</sub> ≪ K<sub>M</sub>: twice C<sub>p</sub>, about twice the rate → first order
C<sub>p</sub> ≫ K<sub>M</sub>: rate ≈ V<sub>max</sub> → zero order

segs.text: When a higher dose raises the level toward saturation of the enzymes, the amount removed per day still rises, but by a smaller fraction than the level rises, so the fraction of the drug in the body removed each day falls. With a smaller fraction removed each day, the half life lengthens and the clearance falls as the dose increases. More of each dose stays in the body, so on her plot of A U C against dose, curve A, the saturable drug, follows the straight line of a drug whose A U C is proportional to dose, curve C, up to a certain dose and then rises above it. Saturation can occur in absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion, and this module deals with elimination.

card.m: into saturation: rate rises less than C<sub>p</sub> → fraction per day ↓
t<sub>½</sub> ↑, Cl ↓ as dose ↑
curve A: above the AUC ∝ dose line past a certain dose
saturable steps: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion; here: elimination

segs.text: On her log plot of level against time, curves A and B are one saturable drug given as a single I V bolus at a high and a low dose, and curve C is a different drug with first order elimination. B is a straight line like C, because at levels well below K M elimination is first order. A starts at levels where the enzymes are saturated, so at first a smaller fraction is removed each hour and A falls less steeply than B; as the level falls, the fraction removed each hour rises and A curves downward. Once A has fallen to levels well below K M it becomes straight, with the same terminal slope as B.

card.m: A: high dose; B: low dose; C: a first-order drug
B straight, like C: C<sub>p</sub> ≪ K<sub>M</sub>, first order
A: saturated at first, smaller fraction per hour → bends
terminal slopes A = B

segs.text: Her slide example shows what this does at steady state, where the daily dose rate equals the elimination rate. At six milligrams per kilogram per day, the steady state level was ten milligrams per liter. Raising the dose rate to eight is one third more, so for a linear drug the level would also rise by one third, to about thirteen milligrams per liter. Instead it rose to twenty milligrams per liter, double, because the enzymes were close to saturated: to remove eight instead of six milligrams per kilogram each day, the level had to climb much higher. She said, Small changes in dose will lead to big changes in concentration.

card.m: steady state: dose rate = elimination rate
6 mg/kg/day → C<sub>ss</sub> 10 mg/L
dose rate × {{frac:8|6}} = × 1.33; linear: 10 mg/L × 1.33 = 13.3 mg/L
8 mg/kg/day → 20 mg/L: dose rate × 1.33, level × 2
small dose change → large level change

segs.text: Her written question asks the difference between linear and nonlinear pharmacokinetics. The answer is the parameters: in linear pharmacokinetics they do not change with dose, and in nonlinear pharmacokinetics increased doses or chronic administration change them. Her signs of saturation are a half life that changes with dose and an A U C that is not in proportion to the dose, plus two more: other drugs needing the same enzyme or carrier can change the saturation, and the ratio of the metabolites can change with dose. In her quiz the true statement was that the half life changes as the dose is increased; parameters that do not change, superposition, and an A U C in proportion to the dose each describe a linear drug.

card.m: linear: parameters fixed; nonlinear: parameters change
signs: t<sub>½</sub> changes, AUC out of proportion, competing drugs, metabolite ratio changes
nonlinear: t½ changes as dose ↑; ✗ fixed parameters, superposition, AUC ∝ dose

segs.text: Her poll said a saturable drug often shows zero order kinetics at low concentrations and first order kinetics at high ones; her key is false, because the orders are the other way round: first order at concentrations well below K M and zero order well above K M. Low and high mean relative to K M, a concentration, never relative to V max, which is a rate. A second trap is to mix up the names: linear pharmacokinetics means first order elimination, not zero order, and a nonlinear drug is first order only at levels well below K M. The summary statement that clearance and half life are usually not constant in nonlinear processes is true. Objective two explains why the order changes with the level.

card.m: poll: zero order at low C, first order at high C? False
low or high: relative to K<sub>M</sub> (mg/L), never V<sub>max</sub> (a rate)
✗ linear = zero order; ✗ nonlinear = first order
Cl and t<sub>½</sub> usually not constant: true
